item.title: Read more about DRC: Ebola is also an information crisis
item.description:
When an Ebola outbreak hits a community, people need reliable information to understand the disease, assess risks and decide where to find care. For journalists, providing this information requires more than reporting the latest case numbers. In eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, misinformation and distrust are creating an additional challenge.

A recent rapid needs assessment by ActionAid DRC across three health zones in Ituri found that only 64% of respondents believed Ebola was a real disease and not linked to spiritual or mystical causes. Only 34% could correctly identify at least three ways Ebola is transmitted. This means journalists are reporting in an environment where basic questions about the disease itself are still contested.

Raoul Kamanda, Director of PNCPS at the Ministry of Health in the DRC, stresses that the way information is communicated matters. He describes how information can either deepen mistrust or help build confidence in the response:“A lot of information can inflame a situation, distort understanding and destroy trust. Other information can build trust and buy-in.”

A long-standing information problem

This is not a new challenge in the DRC. During the 2018-2019 Ebola outbreak in North Kivu, a population-based study found that 92% of respondents had heard at least one common misinformation claim about Ebola. Almost half, 46%, believed at least one of these claims. One in four believed the statement that Ebola did not exist.

Recent monitoring indicates that misinformation remains a big problem during the current outbreak. WHO's Africa Infodemic Response Alliance has documented rumours about safe burial practices and treatment, traditional remedies and the financing of the Ebola response. Raoul Kamanda, Director of the National Program for Communication and Health Promotion (PNCPS) in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and one of the speakers in our upcoming webinar series for journalists covering the outbreak, also points to the role of traditional and religious figures in spreading false information:"There are also traditional healers or pastors who give false testimonies, false prophecies."

These rumours come from genuine questions and concerns. According to the Centre for Information Resilience (CIR), communities in eastern DRC have experienced 17 Ebola outbreaks since 1976, alongside decades of conflict, displacement and resource extraction. The CIR recently examined how this history shapes the current sceptic reponse. Their research points to previous scandals and alleged abuses linked to international aid organisations, as well as low trust in health authorities and international actors. These experiences have created a deep mistrust around Ebola and the people responding to it giving misinformation more room to spread.

These rumours are a real problem for journalists as well. Congolese journalist Tuver Wundi has seen how mis- and disinformation can affect both journalists and the communities they work in: “Yes, there were quite a few [rumours], because people believed journalists were moving around [spreading the disease], Wundi says. “In Nyania, for example, there were protests against the response and journalists were targeted.”

The role of journalists

This makes the work of local journalists especially important. Journalists have to answer difficult questions, verify and debunk competing claims in a context where misinformation is widespread. What exactly is the virus? How does it spread? What information about vaccines and treatment is reliable? How should journalists report on deaths, survivors and burials? And what should they do when a dangerous rumour starts circulating in their community? To answer these journalists need information from reliable sources and specialist knowledge. They also need to protect themselves. Journalists in affected areas also risk their own health.

Reporting on Ebola also requires journalists to understand the medical realities behind the outbreak. Popaul Nunza, Head of Communication at the National Institute for Biomedical Research in the DRC, says the absence of specific treatment for the current strain has created understandable fear.“We had neither therapy nor specific medication for this strain. When you announce a strain with no specific medication, it's frightening. That fear is understandable.” [..]. People are also skeptical. “People kept asking: ‘Why go to the hospital if there's no medicine for this strain?’”, Nunza says.

Supporting journalists on the ground

Free Press Unlimited is supporting journalists covering the Ebola outbreak in eastern DRC through a series of three practical webinars. The webinars bring together Congolese health experts, government officials and experienced journalists to address the questions journalists face when reporting on the outbreak.

The three sessions focus on:

  • Understanding the disease
  • Staying safe as a journalist in an affected area
  • Reporting accurately and ethically

The discussions will cover both the medical and journalistic challenges of reporting on Ebola. This includes understanding how the virus spreads, identifying reliable information about treatment and vaccines, staying safe while reporting from affected areas, and dealing with rumours and misinformation.

More information about the webinars (in French)

Following the webinars, Free Press Unlimited will publish a series of practical training manuals covering the same three topics. The manuals are being developed together with Congolese infectious disease and public health experts, senior Ministry of Health officials and journalists covering the outbreak. The manuals will be available in French, Swahili and Lingala, giving journalists access to the information and practical guidance beyond the live sessions.

Reliable information matters

During an Ebola outbreak, journalists need access to reliable information and practical guidance to report accurately and responsibly. By bringing together experts and journalists through the webinars and making the knowledge available through practical training manuals, Free Press Unlimited is supporting journalists who are reporting on the outbreak in eastern DRC.

item.title: Read more about CPJ review confirms: Israel still responsible for majority of killings of journalists and media workers worldwide since 2023
item.description:
The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) has documented the killing of journalists and media workers in Israel and the occupied Palestinian territory since October 7, 2023. In June 2026, CPJ announced a comprehensive review of its database after Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad published obituaries identifying as combatants a number of individuals whom CPJ had documented as journalists or media workers. 

Free Press Unlimited commends CPJ’s efforts to review cases and keep improving its database, when credible new information becomes available. It shows commitment to continuous improvement of their data, which increases trustworthiness.

The first phase of the review, covering 229 cases, was completed in July and its findings were presented in a confidential internal report on July 7. CPJ subsequently commissioned an external audit to assess the review’s process and findings. The findings of the review and audit were published on September 24.

Scale of journalist killings unparalleled

As a result of new information obtained through the review, CPJ removed 22 individuals previously listed as journalists or media workers from its database: newly surfaced information identified 19 individuals as combatants, while the remaining three were found to be non-journalist civilians. CPJ also reinstated six individuals and reclassified 12 cases from journalist to media worker, or vice versa. Even after these changes, the scale of journalist killings in the conflict remains unparalleled.

FPU supports CPJ’s intention to commission an external International Humanitarian Law expert to review its criteria concerning work in military media units and publish the findings. In situations of armed conflict, determining whether an individual is participating in hostilities is highly complex and directly relevant to the protections afforded to journalists as civilians under international humanitarian law.

No justice

Not a single of the 191 journalist killings has resulted in justice, despite promises of investigations. No attack on any journalist should go unpunished. Despite this impunity, journalists in Palestine continue their work resiliently. As Al Jazeera journalist Anas Al Sharif wrote in his farewell message, when he was expecting to get killed: “I have lived through pain in all its details, tasted suffering and loss many times, yet I never once hesitated to convey the truth as it is, without distortion or falsification. [...] I urge you not to let chains silence you, nor borders restrain you.”

Read the full audit by CPJ here.

item.title: Read more about Nominations for the Free Press Awards 2026 are now open
item.description:
Once again, Free Press Unlimited is looking for journalists whose work demonstrates courage, perseverance and a strong commitment to independent journalism. The Free Press Awards recognise outstanding journalists in two categories: Most Resilient Journalist and Newcomer of the Year. Nominations for the 2026 edition are now open.

Last year, the awards recognised two journalists who continued their work under extreme circumstances. Azerbaijani journalist Ulviyya Guliyeva received the Most Resilient Journalist Award, while Sudanese journalist AlMigdad Hassan was named Newcomer of the Year. Their stories show the courage and commitment these awards seek to recognise. 

Do you know a journalist whose work deserves recognition? Nominate them for a Free Press Award 2026.

Newcomer of the Year, Hans Verploeg Award

This award recognises a promising journalist with a maximum of four years of experience. We are looking for emerging talent with a strong commitment to independent journalism and press freedom. The winner receives a media scholarship.

Most Resilient Journalist

This award honours a journalist who continues to report despite serious pressure, threats or other difficult circumstances. The winner receives a cash prize.

Deadline for nominations: 16 October 2026

For more information and to nominate candidates go to this page.

Criteria for nomination

Nominations are reviewed by an independent panel of international experts.

• You cannot nominate yourself.
• The nominee must be aware of and agree with the nomination.
• Please submit at least three examples of the nominee’s work.
• For Newcomer of the Year, the nominee must have a maximum of four years of experience as a journalist.

Previous winners

Most Resilient Journalist

  • Ulviyya Guliyeva, Azerbaijan, 2025
  • Dicle Müftüoğlu, Turkey, 2023
  • The late Mantas Kvedaravičius, Lithuania, 2022
  • Rozina Islam, Bangladesh, 2021
  • Maria Ressa, Philippines, 2020

item.title: Read more about Emergency Media Support Grants: Call for Proposals for SMF Members
item.description:
Media and CSOs actors are operating under severe disruption, including displacement, safety risks, infrastructure breakdown, and censorship pressures. This small support mechanism is designed to contribute stabilizing essential work that protects the public’s access to verified information, that help reducing harm, and supports social cohesion.

This is an internal call managed by FPU in close coordination with Norwegian embassy for benefit of SMF members and open exclusively to eligible SMF member organisations. 

FPU expects to award 5 grants of up to €20,000 each, for a grant period of six (6) months, subject to the urgency and quality of applications. A total of three grants will be awarded to media outlets, and two will be allocated to non-media organizations.

Priority is given to proposals that demonstrate clear public interest value, strong feasibility under current conditions, and responsible communication (NGOs) or journalism (media organisations) practices.

Objectives of the support

The grants aim to support initiatives that:

  • Helps essential public-interest media production to continue
  • Counter misinformation and harmful narratives
  • Promote conflict-sensitive and constructive journalism
  • Serve audiences affected by displacement or insecurity
  • Strengthen collaboration and resilience within the media ecosystem
  • Amplify community voices 

Urgency is treated as a universal threshold condition. Comparative assessment focuses on preventing the greatest immediate harm to public access to reliable information.

Who can apply

Eligible applicants must:

  • Be an SMF member organisation in good standing
  • Demonstrate operational capacity to implement activities safely
  • Meet minimum editorial and ethical standards
  • Show ability to reach intended audiences/constituencies under current conditions

Applications that fail minimum capacity or content safeguards will not proceed to scoring.

What we support

Support will be provided based on:

Media organisations: 

  • Urgent operational needs: Current operational challenges requiring immediate financial or technical support to resume or sustain production.
  • Public interest journalism: Alignment with call objectives including countering misinformation, civic awareness, and addressing Sudan's current context of conflict, displacement, governance, and humanitarian issues.
  • Meaningful impact: Ability to produce impactful content that supports democratic dialogue and reaches Sudanese audiences, particularly in exile or conflict-affected areas. 

Non-media organisations: 

  • Capacity to positively advocate for change: Have a clear advocacy strategy to support peace, democracy and freedom.
  • Have a coherent capacity to strengthen media organizations through training and capacity building, as fitting the needs of members of the SMF. 

Types of activities supported

Proposals may include, for example:

  • Emergency continuation of news or public-interest reporting/ community engagement
  • Fact-checking or counter-disinformation content
  • Community information services
  • Collaborative reporting initiatives
  • Content/Activities that promotes cohesion or reduces harmful narratives
  • Advocacy activities 
  • Activities that focus on capacity building, such as a hands on specialised workshops, series of thematic webinars, peer to peer learning, etc. 

Activities must be feasible, safety-aware, and conflict-sensitive.

Evaluation criteria and weights

Applications are reviewed through a structured, independent process using published criteria. The evaluation considers the following criteria with specified weights totaling 100%:

  • Relevance and Alignment (20%)
    Alignment with call objectives, relevance to the current Sudanese context, and clear target audience identification.
  • Technical and Operational Capacity (20%)
    Realistic timeline and workplan, team capacity, access to platforms and audiences, past performance, and risk mitigation.
  • Diversity and Inclusion Contribution (20%)
    Inclusion of women, youth, minorities, or displaced populations; gender sensitive and inclusive content; local language or community outreach.
  • Partnership and Collaboration Potential (15%)
    Ability to build bridges and work across divides.
  • Budget and Value for Money (10%)
    Budget clarity and realism, cost effectiveness, and appropriate allocation to content.
  • Ethical and Accountability Standards (15%)
    Accuracy and verification, responsible language and framing, conflict sensitivity, ethical safeguards, and balanced representation of voices.

A minimum threshold score is required to advance.

Decision Process

Eligible proposals are reviewed by an independent jury using standardized scoring tools. 

Each proposal will be assessed by multiple independent reviewers to ensure consistency and fairness. 

Timeline

Call Announcement: 10 September 2026 

Application Deadline: 24 September 2026 

Eligibility check: 28 September 2026

Review Period: 29 September- 16 October 2026 

Award communication: 19 October 2026

How to apply

Applicants must submit:

  • Completed proposal form that includes description and implementation plan, Safety and risk considerations
  • Budget outline

Apply now

Contact and questions

For questions, clarifications, or support with your application, before 24 September, please ask here: info@freepressunlimited.org

Please submit your questions before the application deadline.

Complaint mechanism

SMF and FPU are committed to a fair and transparent selection process. Applicants who believe a procedural concern has arisen are encouraged to raise it through the mechanism described below.

What can be raised. Complaints may relate to eligibility rules not applied as published, undisclosed conflicts of interest, procedural errors or deviations, breaches of confidentiality or ethics, or discriminatory conduct in the process.

What cannot be appealed. This mechanism covers process integrity only. Disagreements with scores, rankings, or jury judgments, as well as concerns about funding availability or pre-set strategic priorities, are not admissible.

How to submit a complaint. Complaints must be submitted in writing to the Secretariat at issues@freepressunlimited.org within 10 working days after receiving the notification letters. Anonymous complaints may be considered where they raise serious misconduct concerns.

What to expect. The Secretariat will acknowledge receipt within 3 working days and provide a full response within 15 working days. Identities of all parties involved are protected throughout the process. Retaliation against complainants is strictly prohibited.

A full version of the Formal Complaints and Appeals Policy is available upon request to FPU.

FAQs

Sudan Media Forum is a coalition of independent media organizations, journalists and aligned CSOs in Sudan. Dedicated to fostering a robust and independent media landscape, the Forum works tirelessly to advance press freedom, promote ethical journalism, and cultivate informed citizenship within a
just and democratic society.


Find out more on the SMF website

Free Press Unlimited is an international press freedom organisation that collaborates with over 300 media partners worldwide. With them, we work on our mission to make independent news and information available to everyone.


Find out more about FPU’s mission on the website

SMF is the partner in outreach and member coordination. FPU is the contracting organization responsible for this call, including eligibility checks, jury coordination, and issuing contracts.

The emergency support grants are institutional grants directed at SMF member organizations.

You can find a complete list of the media outlets on this page. If you are still in doubt, please reach out to your editor-in-chief.

You will be required to insert an email once you start the Google Form. Please make sure the email is valid and one that you frequently access. Once you complete the Google Form, you will receive a confirmation on said e-mail with a copy of your answers.

The Google Form is formulated in a way that every question has an explanation; however, if you experience troubles please reach out to info@freepressunlimited.org and indicate ‘Application for ‘SMF Emergency Media Production Support’.

Please fill in every box that applies to your organisation. If a box genuinely doesn't apply (for example, you're not requesting equipment), write "N/A" rather than leaving it blank.

The form is bilingual so either language reader can review it, but you only need to write your answers once, in whichever language you're most comfortable in.

The applications are evaluated by a Jury composed of 3 members. All jury members have committed to the utmost professionalism and are selected and operaring to avoid any conflicts of interest.


The SMF board is not involved in evaluating applications or deciding awards. If you have a question about your application or the process, contact FPU directly at info@freepressunlimited.org, not the SMF board.

The results of the call will be communicated on 19 October. However, the Jury reserved itself the right to postpone the date in case of an unexpected number of applications or unforseen delays.

Submit a written complaint to issues@freepressunlimited.org within 10 working days of the notification that triggered the concern.


The Secretariat will acknowledge within 3 working days and respond in full within 15 working days. Your identity is protected. Note that disagreements with jury scores or rankings are not admissible

  • Budget and Value for Money (10%)

item.description:
On 26 August 2026, several devastating floods struck five districts in Nepal: Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Chitwan and Gorkha. The floods significantly damaged or destroyed homes, public buildings and essential services. The disaster also has significant impact on journalists and media outlets in Rasuwa and Nuwakot and keeping their communities informed.

Journalists have lost family members, homes, vehicles. Some journalists are still missing, while others are working with damaged equipment with no electricity and internet connections.

We are in direct contact with a media organisation on the ground, Freedom Forum. They found that four journalists are missing and around 14 family members of journalists are missing. Two journalists lost their vehicles. Six community radio stations are dealing with irregular electricity and internet connections.

Local journalists continue to report

Despite the impact of the floods on their own lives and work, journalists in affected areas continue to provide information to the public. Shiva Devkota, a journalist in Nuwakot, lost his office motorcycle in the flood. The loss has made it harder for him to travel to gather news.

“This has caused problems in my daily commute to gather news reports. This has directly affected access to information,” he says.

Journalists in Nuwakot continue to share information about search and rescue efforts, relief operations and other developments despite the circumstances they are facing themselves.

“We have continued to provide people with vital information”

Local radio stations have also been affected by the disruption caused by the floods. Radio Langtang still doesn’t have proper internet access. While media did not suffer major physical damage, the local market area was swept away, affecting the station's main sources of advertising revenue.

“We have continued to provide people with vital information during this crisis, but our own future remains uncertain,” says station manager Geeta Neupane.

Other radio stations face different challenges. Radio Trishuli has experienced technical problems caused by frequent power outages. At Radio Jalapa, floodwater entered the studio and damaged (back-up) batteries, UPS equipment and other equipment. Radio Chimteshwor is in dire need of satellite communication equipment, laptops, shelter and solar power.

Nuwakot FM deals with a damaged fibre connection and equipment. Around 2.9 kilometres of fibre was damaged, while equipment including a mixer, UPS, batteries, laptops, camera, uplink device and connectors was completely destroyed. The station has since managed to resume broadcasting after repairs to the fibre.

Nuwakot FM’s optic fibre damaged after the flood

Losing equipment

Kiran Adhikari, editor of Sundaradevi Sandesh Weekly in Nuwakot, lost his residence, media archives and reporting equipment in the flood.

“The day I myself became a victim, I lost all my property. Losing my property is okay, I can stand and earn again. But all the personal documents, data, newspaper archives I had collected since I started journalism were also swept away.”

Two laptops were also lost. Kiran says the documents and materials he collected since he began journalism cannot be recovered. Kiran is currently living with his family in Kathmandu with support of relatives and fellow journalists. His primary needs to continue his work are access to internet, means of transportation, a laptop, a power bank and temporary shelter.

Reporting after losing a home

Journalist Sunny Shrestha also lost his house and land in Nuwakot due to the floods. Despite losing his own property, he travelled to Rasuwa with colleagues to report on the situation and bring the experiences of affected people to the government.

“Even though I had lost everything myself, I did not want to sit around feeling helpless. Even though there was no pressure from my office to return to work, I wanted to bring voices and experiences of those affected to reach the government.”

Sunny's current needs include temporary shelter, a camera, laptop, power bank and financial support.

Sunny Shresta standing where his house used to be

Supporting local journalism

Freedom Forum's assessment shows that the impact of the Nepal floods on journalists and media outlets can vary. Some journalists have lost homes and property. Others have lost vehicles or essential work equipment. Radio stations are dealing with disrupted electricity and internet connections, while some media outlets face the longer-term effects of damage to local economies. The support needs identified are clear: laptops, power banks, internet and communication devices, backup power, transportation and temporary working spaces.

Free Press Unlimited supports affected journalists and newsrooms in Nepal. Your donation helps journalists directly by giving them the means to continue their work and help communities access to reliable information.

item.title: Read more about AI-Driven Violence Threatens Journalists’ Safety and Press Freedom
item.description:
With the development of Artificial Intelligence (AI), online violence against journalists has taken a new turn. The online environment was already unsafe for journalists, but now AI acts as a catalyst for online harassment, intimidation, and subversion. This development not only hinders their work but also jeopardizes press freedom and the underlying democratic processes in general. Public awareness of this issue is needed to make progress in the areas of legislation and enforcement, as the role that AI plays in online violence has not yet been universally recognized by law at the European level. With this in mind, Free Press Unlimited delved into the world of artificial intelligence. In what ways is AI being used to attack journalists? What does AI-facilitated violence look like today? And what patterns can be identified?

AI facilitates existing forms of online violence against journalists, such as identity fraud, threats, and sexual violence. That is why we refer to “AI-facilitated violence” in this article. This includes so-called deepfakes: AI-generated videos, photos, or audio clips that are difficult to distinguish from real footage. Free Press Unlimited identified a total of 58 incidents within the MMF Monitor in which AI was used to obstruct or intimidate journalists. The MFRR’s Mapping Media Freedom (MMF) Monitor is a European database where journalists report incidents in which they were targeted. The incidents all took place in Europe between 2022 and 2026.

AI-Facilitated Scams

One primary form of AI use is the so-called AI-facilitated “scam.” In this scenario, the journalist’s reputation or expertise is exploited to promote a scam. Seventeen of the 58 incidents investigated fall into this category. This development undermines the credibility and expertise of journalists. In the fintech sector, where new technology is being developed for the financial world, deepfake scams rose by 700% in 2023.

One example is the case of Gabriel Mellqvist, a Swedish journalist who covers financial news. An AI-generated fake advertisement for an investment platform pretended that he was endorsing it. As a result, approximately 500 investors were defrauded, with a total loss of about 500 million Swedish kronor (approximately 46 million euros). The journalist himself says he is frustrated that his reputation has been damaged by this incident.
 

AI-Facilitated Russian Disinformation

A second category consists of Russian disinformation campaigns. These campaigns use personas of journalists (and sometimes entire news websites) to spread pro-Russian or anti-Ukrainian narratives. These disinformation campaigns are known by various names, such as Portal Kombat, Storm 15-16, Matryoshka (Overload), and Doppelganger. Sixteen of the 58 cases investigated can be linked to Russian disinformation strategies.

The case of French news anchor Julien Fanciulli, who works for France24, illustrates how one of these campaigns, Portal Kombat (also known as the “Pravda network”), operates. In 2024, a deepfake video of Fanciulli was published by pravda.fr and further disseminated by various pro-Russian information portals. In the deepfake video, Fanciulli, appearing as a France24 news anchor, reported that President Macron had postponed his trip to Kyiv due to a planned assassination attempt on the president. This narrative casts doubt on Western confidence in Ukraine by portraying Kyiv as unsafe.

The French intelligence agency VIGNIUM describes Portal Kombat as a network of news portals comprising at least 193 affiliated websites. They do not produce original content but re-post information from pro-Russian social media accounts and news channels to reach a Western audience. In addition, Storm 15-16, Matryoshka, and Doppelganger are characterized as “information laundering.” This means that disinformation is posted and disseminated on a massive scale, in part thanks to AI, so that its origin becomes unrecognizable. 

Since July 2023, more than 8 million fake articles have been re-posted by the Pravda Network, according to the monitoring website portal-kombat.com, an initiative of the fact-checking organization Checkfirst. In addition, Matryoshka is particularly known for spreading AI deepfakes. Doppelganger mimics official news websites, sometimes using AI-generated content. Behind these websites are organizations funded by the Russian government.


Sexual Violence

A third category consists of sexual deepfakes. In these cases, AI is used to generate sexual images of journalists without their consent. Five of the 58 analyzed incidents fall into this category. Deepfakes are increasing rapidly. In 2023, there were an estimated 500,000 deepfakes online; according to a forecast, this number rose to 8 million by 2025. As many as 96–98% of all deepfakes consist of non-consensual sexual content online, with women being the victims in 99% of cases. The societal consequences of online gender-based violence are far-reaching. For example, previous research has shown that women may withdraw from the public sphere or be unable to continue practicing their profession.

Free Press Unlimited observes that the dissemination of this type of imagery can damage a journalist’s reputation or lead to further online, and sometimes physical, intimidation. The psychological harm suffered by victims can be comparable to that caused by physical sexual violence. Furthermore, AI-generated images are difficult to remove from the internet. These images can continue to cause harm long after their publication.

With relatively little effort, Free Press Unlimited found websites featuring explicit deepfakes of thirteen Dutch women, including three journalists. For privacy reasons, we have decided not to disclose the URLs of these websites. Under Dutch law, the distribution of non-consensual sexual deepfakes is prohibited. Nevertheless, illegal content featuring Dutch journalists is still online as of the writing of this article. In May 2026, NRC revealed that AI-generated porn websites are also hosted on Dutch territory, such as the website “Motherless.”

In Italy, too, two well-known female journalists and presenters fell victim to this. Francesca Barra and Selvaggia Lucarelli found AI-generated nude images of themselves on a website with millions of users that features multiple (well-known) women. Although the Italian police launched an investigation after this incident came to light, this website is also still online.


AI-facilitated political intimidation

The final category consists of journalists who have been targeted by an AI-facilitated political attack. They are known for their political convictions and have often been the target of physical or online violence in the past. The intimidation has a clear political motive. item.title: Read more about Independent media are a core player for Europe’s democratic resilience
item.description:
Foreign interference, disinformation and AI manipulation are becoming common practice and their putting increasing pressure on European democracies. To fight these and other foreign and domestic threats to European democracies, the EU is establishing the European Centre for Democratic Resilience (ECDR). An important step, but it will only deliver to its promises if independent media are recognised as part of the solution.

European democracies face increased pressures due to rising geopolitical tensions, conflict, autocracy and technology. To render European democracies resilient to these threats, the European Commission has announced the foundation of the European Centre for Democratic Resilience (ECDR).

Journalists are often the first to uncover information manipulation, expose foreign influence and hold those in power to account. In doing so, they face serious attacks and intimidation. For example, Moldova’s largest investigative news outlet Ziarul de Gardă exposed Russia’s illegal financing of digital and online armies to hijack the elections. Yet too often, discussions about democratic resilience focus on governments and technology, while the role of independent journalism is overlooked.

On June 23, 2026, Free Press Unlimited (FPU) and ARTICLE 19 Europe brought together EU policymakers, experts, journalists and civil society organisations at the European Parliament to talk about this. What should the design and mandate of the new ECDR look like? How should media be included in the ECDR and how should the role of independent journalism be incorporated in its activities to protect democratic resilience?

The discussion highlighted several recommendations, including on independent media:

  • Make the whole-of-society approach a reality: Independent journalists and media organisations must be included in the multi-stakeholder platform and recognised as essential partners in protecting democratic resilience. They should be consulted in a regular, inclusive and meaningful way.
  • Focus on prevention, not just response: It’s not enough to only fight disinformation after it has spread. Investing in media freedom at the domestic level, investigative media that can expose and prebunk disinformation tailored to local context, and media literacy and access to reliable information to empower European citizens renders societies more resilient to future threats.
  • Protect the ECDR from political influence: The Centre should include strong safeguards to make sure it remains independent and free from governments or political interests. For example, efforts to address disinformation and FIMI should not be at the expense of media freedom and freedom of expression.

These recommendations will be the basis of follow-up discussions on the development of the ECDR and the wider European Democracy Shield. FPU will continue to advocate for independent journalism to be recognised as a cornerstone of democratic resilience. Not just as an afterthought.

item.title: Read more about Press freedom in France under growing pressure ahead of 2027 elections
item.description:
Free Press Unlimited is warning that press freedom in France is coming under increasing pressure ahead of the 2027 presidential elections. As part of a joint mission by the Media Freedom Rapid Response (MFRR), a coalition of European press freedom organisations, we identified growing media concentration, the mainstreaming of far-right narratives, deficient anti-SLAPP legislation, and the need for stronger support for journalists in exile as some of the most pressing concerns.

Media ownership threatens pluralism

One of the mission's main findings is concerning media concentration. Today, around 90% of France's national media is controlled by just a handful of industrial groups. This threatens media pluralism and increases the risk of political and commercial influence over editorial decisions, particularly in the run-up to the 2027 elections. The MFRR calls on France to modernise its media ownership laws and fully implement the European Media Freedom Act (EMFA).

Growing concerns ahead of the 2027 elections

We also warn that political interference in newsrooms and the growing influence of media owners have contributed to the mainstreaming of far-right narratives in parts of the French media landscape, including hostile rhetoric towards journalists and public services media. With political polarisation on the rise, safeguarding independent journalism is more important than ever to protect democratic debate.

Inadequate anti-SLAPP protections

We also found that lawsuits that aim to silence journalists under the pretext of ‘fake news’ have increased significantly, particularly initiated by local far-right politicians. Despite this concerning development, France’s implementation of the EU Anti-SLAPP Directive falls short of protecting journalists and other public watchdogs from abusive lawsuits. New legislation offer some protection, but it applies only to civil proceedings. Criminal defamation cases – one of the most common legal tools used to intimidate journalists in France – remain out of scope.

France must do more to protect exiled journalists

It is positive that France hosts one of the largest communities of journalists in exile in Europe. During the mission, the MFRR delegation met with journalists from Tunisia, Afghanistan, Benin, Algeria, Guinea, Egypt, Yemen, Pakistan and Haiti to hear about their experiences. Many described how transnational repression continues to affect them even after fleeing their home countries. They also spoke about the difficulties of continuing their journalist profession after arriving in France.

We call for stronger support for journalists in exile. This includes better protection against transnational repression, language and professional training, stronger links with French newsrooms, psycho-social support, and closer cooperation between organisations and public authorities.

Other concerns

We also raised concerns about the safety of journalists reporting from protests, insufficient protection of journalists' sources, and the delayed implementation of the European Media Freedom Act (EMFA). Together, these challenges paint a worrying picture of the state of press freedom in France.

Read the full MFRR mission statement here

item.title: Read more about Free Press Unlimited and partners urge Indonesian president to reopen investigation into journalist's murder
item.description:
Free Press Unlimited (FPU), together with the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) and five other civil society organisations, has called on Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto to order a new investigation into the murder of journalist Rico Sempurna Pasaribu and his family.

The joint letter follows the publication of the recent CPJ–FPU investigation, Impunity in Indonesia: The leads left unfollowed in journalist Rico Sempurna Pasaribu's murder, which uncovered serious flaws in the official investigation and presented substantial evidence that active-duty soldier Corporal Herman Bukit should be thoroughly investigated for his alleged role in the killings.

Pasaribu, a journalist with Tribrata TV, was killed alongside his wife, son and grandson in an arson attack on their home in North Sumatra on 27 June 2024. Before the attack, he had received threats after reporting on an alleged illegal gambling operation linked to Bukit.

In the letter, the organisations call on the Indonesian authorities to reopen the investigation, ensure that any prosecution takes place before a civilian court, and conduct a transparent and impartial investigation that examines all available evidence. They argue that the previous investigation failed to properly investigate key leads and overlooked evidence pointing to Bukit's possible involvement.

The letter was also sent to the chief of the Indonesian National Police, the commander of the Indonesian National Armed Forces, and Commission 1 of the Indonesian House of Representatives.

Free Press Unlimited (FPU), together with the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) and five other civil society organisations, has called on Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto to order a new investigation into the murder of journalist Rico Sempurna Pasaribu and his family.

The joint letter follows the publication of the recent CPJ–FPU investigation, Impunity in Indonesia: The leads left unfollowed in journalist Rico Sempurna Pasaribu's murder, which uncovered serious flaws in the official investigation and presented substantial evidence that active-duty soldier Corporal Herman Bukit should be thoroughly investigated for his alleged role in the killings.

Pasaribu, a journalist with Tribrata TV, was killed alongside his wife, son and grandson in an arson attack on their home in North Sumatra on 27 June 2024. Before the attack, he had received threats after reporting on an alleged illegal gambling operation linked to Bukit.

In the letter, the organisations call on the Indonesian authorities to reopen the investigation, ensure that any prosecution takes place before a civilian court, and conduct a transparent and impartial investigation that examines all available evidence. They argue that the previous investigation failed to properly investigate key leads and overlooked evidence pointing to Bukit's possible involvement.

The letter was also sent to the chief of the Indonesian National Police, the commander of the Indonesian National Armed Forces, and Commission 1 of the Indonesian House of Representatives.

item.description:
While the EU strengthens its partnership with Vietnam, Vietnamese authorities are increasingly targeting critics beyond their own borders. Journalists, human rights defenders and political dissidents living in Thailand face significant pressure, such as: surveillance, intimidation, arbitrary detention and the risk of being returned to Vietnam by force.

Journalists at risk

Independent Vietnamese journalists in exile are often targeted. Many of them continue to report despite ongoing threats and harassment. Even after fleeing Vietnam, they are forced to stay vigilant and keep a low profile.

In the joint statement we highlights the cases of journalists Truong Duy Nhat and Duong Van Thai. Both disappeared in Thailand before reappearing in Vietnamese custody. They were later sentenced to lengthy prison terms. The coalition says these cases show how Vietnam reaches across borders to silence independent voices.

Growing concerns

We are also concerned about plans for a new extradition treaty between Thailand and Vietnam. Without strong human rights safeguards, such an agreement could make it easier to arrest and return political dissidents under the guise of criminal cooperation.

At the same time, activists report increased surveillance and intimidation in Thailand. Refugee communities say they are being closely monitored, creating fear among those who fled persecution in Vietnam.

What the EU should do

The coalition calls on the EU to:

  • Raise transnational repression in all political and human rights dialogues with Vietnam and Thailand, and make it a priority across diplomatic engagement.
  • Hold Vietnamese and Thai officials accountable for human rights violations, and make clear that transnational repression is incompatible with the EU's partnership with Vietnam.
  • Press for transparency in the negotiations on the extradition treaty and mutual legal assistance treaty. Any agreement should include strong safeguards against politically motivated extraditions and uphold the principle of non-refoulement.
  • Strengthen protection through EU delegations and member state embassies by monitoring cases, engaging with at-risk communities and publicly speaking out against cross-border repression.
  • Expand emergency visas and resettlement opportunities for journalists, human rights defenders and other activists at risk in Thailand.
  • Publicly condemn Vietnam's misuse of national security and other laws to target journalists, activists and government critics.
  • Ensure EU cooperation on digital technologies does not enable surveillance or other forms of digital transnational repression, while supporting digital security for journalists and activists at risk.

Together with the coalition, we ask the EU to make clear that transnational repression has no place in its partnership with Vietnam. Protecting journalists and others at risk should remain a central part of that relationship. Read the full statement below:
